title: Line Kit
description: Stamp points, draw straight strokes through them, cap every end with a dot or an arrowhead, and find the two rays that start at a point on a line.
modes: none. One flow, one phase at a time. The host mounts a phase (phase prop). With navigableDots true, or no phase, the child may jump phases with the dots (user mode); otherwise the dots show progress and the teacher agent drives window.toolApi (AI mode). The last phase, and a whole lesson, end on the summary page, where Free play and Play again sit.

stage.sizing: the frame is min(100vw, 177.78vh) wide and min(100vh, 56.25vw) tall (dvh where supported); the svg fills it. Nothing scrolls.

bands.header: 0 to 80. One line: the tool name, a measured dot, the phase concept; again, sound and restart as round controls far right.
bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded card holding the running count, the working area, the question, the answer box and the keypad; the summary page covers it at the end.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The mascot at the far left on its ground line, the speech bubble beside it, the phase dots and the phase and question counts at the right.

zones.controls: circles r 28 at cx 1388, 1460, 1532, cy 40: again, sound, restart; 72-unit finger boxes
zones.dots: one pill per phase across bar, pitch 158; in user mode each is a button with a 72-tall finger box

stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box on the stage. The score leaves on finished and onComplete and is shown once, as stars on the summary page.

writeup.why: Put points down and name them, draw straight strokes through them, and let the ends of each stroke say whether it stops or carries on.
writeup.look: A drawing board with a point stamp, a ruler that turns to any slope, a tray of dots and arrowheads, and a tape measure coiled at one corner.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Line Kit' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the points named, the ends capped or the rays named, against what this phase lays out, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each point takes its letter, each end takes its cap or each ray settles in the name strip, and the second fixed at what this phase holds. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The tool column stands at the left of the working area, 140 by 500 at 64,214: the point stamp at its top, 140 by 90, and the letter tray under it at 64,316, the twenty-six capitals in rows of four, a letter already on the board dimmed in the tray so that no letter can name two points. The magnifier rests at the foot of the column, a round glass 120 across at 74,590. The drawing board fills the middle, 780 by 440 at 220,214, on the panel colour. A stamp puts down one vermilion dot, every dot on the board the same small size, and the curve pen joins named points in the order they are tapped with one freehand deep blue curve. The ruler lies across the board and turns about its middle to any slope; laid through two points it draws one straight deep blue stroke through both, and each end of the stroke waits in an open socket for a cap. The cap tray stands at the right, 134 by 180 at 1016,214, holding vermilion dots and deep blue arrowheads: two dots make a line segment, a dot and an arrowhead a ray, and two arrowheads a line, and a stroke with an open socket is never named. The tape is coiled under the cap tray, 134 by 90 at 1016,410, and unrolls in amber along any stroke from its first end: at a dot it stops and reads the length in centimetres, and at an arrowhead it runs on past the edge of the board with its reading left blank. The ray splitter sits under the tape, 134 by 70 at 1016,516, and works only on a point that sits on a line: tapped there, it lights the line from that point one way to its arrowhead, thick in deep blue, and then the other way in sky blue, the second thing set beside the first. The name strip runs along the foot of the board, 780 by 56 at 220,666, and writes each stroke's name as its second cap lands and each ray's name, starting letter first, as the splitter lights it. The magnifier, passed over a point, spreads the grain of the paper apart under the glass while the dot is redrawn at its one small size. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is a word pad of the twenty-six capitals wherever a point, a stroke or a ray is named, with three keys under them reading line, line segment and ray. Wherever a length or a count is asked for it is twelve number keys three across, with a key beside them reading no length, so a line or a ray is answered by press and never with a number. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own and are the pictures' colours too. The figure being studied, every line, segment, ray, side, outline, circle, angle arm and visible edge of a solid, is deep blue. Every point, end point, corner dot, vertex dot and the centre dot of a circle is vermilion. A length being measured, walked, added or named, and every angle arc and square corner mark, is amber. The unit squares that cover an area, the flood inside a closed figure and a face of a solid being counted are green. A line of symmetry or a mirror line is reddish purple and always dotted. The second thing set beside the first, a fold being tried, a mirror image, the other half of a fold, a chord that is not a diameter and the larger angle between clock hands, is sky blue. A hidden edge of a solid is grey and dashed, and grey is used for nothing else. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome: every grid line, ruler tick, bracket, guide line and table rule is near-black. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a point is a round dot, a line carries an arrowhead at each end, a ray a dot and one arrowhead and a segment a dot at each end, a measured length carries its number, a hidden edge is dashed and a line of symmetry is dotted, before any of them is told by a colour. A dotted line always means a true line of symmetry or a mirror line, and a fold being tried is drawn solid until it is kept, so nothing else on any stage of this chapter is ever dotted. A point is one small dot everywhere on this stage and never grows, whatever the magnifier does to the paper round it. No stroke is ever left with a bare end that could be read either way: until its cap lands, an end shows an open socket, and the stroke carries no name.
writeup.finish: The card shows the board the child drew on, every stroke with its caps and its name, and the rays they found lit from the point they tapped.

phases.win: the paper spreads apart under the magnifier while the dot stays one small mark, and the curve runs through every named point in order
phases.does: stamps points, names each one with a capital letter, passes the magnifier over one, then joins them in order with the curve pen
phases.goal: a point marks a position, has no size, and is named by a capital letter
phases.says: Put a point down and give it a name. Look closer. Does it get any bigger?
phases.check: Away from the screen: mark three points on paper, one of them a fat dot, and name each. How big is each point?
phases.feels: the dot can grow as big as the ink likes, and the place it marks never grows at all
phases.hands: Draw a small chalk dot on the board and name it A. Draw a much fatter dot beside it and name it B. Ask which point is bigger, then ask a child to put a fingertip on exactly the place A marks, and on exactly the place B marks. Last, mark six dots across the board, name them in order and join them with one freehand curve.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: what does the dot show? Second rung, the phase's: does the place grow when the ink does? Third rung: the board is cut to one named point, and the magnifier passes over it before the second point comes back. The letter pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: on paper a dot is the only thing anyone ever sees of a point, so the size of the ink looks like the size of the point.
wrong.move: calls the point drawn as a fat dot the bigger point.
wrong.screen: the magnifier passes over each dot in turn, and under the glass the paper spreads apart while the exact place each dot marks is found at its middle and held there as one small mark. The two places are restamped side by side at the board's one small size, the fat ink left faintly behind the second, and the child's answer stays in the slot with nothing marked.

wrong.why: a letter used across the board looks free once its point is out of sight, and any letter seems to do as a name.
wrong.move: gives a second point the letter already standing on the first, so one letter names two places.
wrong.screen: the letter tray holds that capital dimmed, and the two points the child meant to share it are lit one after the other while the dimmed letter pulses. A free capital is offered beside the second point, and the child's name stays written in the strip beside it until another is chosen.

phases.screen: an empty drawing board with the point stamp, the letter tray and the magnifier waiting
phases.soWhat: A point marks a place and has no size. It is shown by a dot and named by a capital letter.

phases.win: the tape runs off both edges of the board without finding an end, and the line is named by its two points
phases.does: draws a straight stroke through both points, caps both ends with arrowheads, turns the ruler to draw lines across, upright and slanting, then runs the tape along one
phases.goal: a line is straight, has an arrowhead at each end, and has no length that can be measured
phases.says: Draw it straight through both points. Now run the tape along it. Where does it stop?
phases.check: Draw one line across, one upright and one slanting, and name each by two points on it. How many arrowheads did you draw?
phases.feels: the arrowheads are not where the line ends, they are the line saying it does not end
phases.hands: Stretch a string across the room and tape a card arrowhead to each end. Ask where the line stops. Then mark C and D on the board, lay a ruler through them and draw one straight stroke with an arrowhead at each end. Draw a line across, one upright and one slanting, and ask how long each one is.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what is at each end of the stroke? Second rung, the phase's: where does the tape stop? Third rung: the board is cut to one line across, and the tape runs along it before the upright and slanting lines come back. The letter pad and the no length key stay open.

wrong.why: a stroke on paper has to stop somewhere, and a dot is the tidy way to finish a stroke off.
wrong.move: caps a line with a dot at each end, so what was meant to be line CD is drawn as a stroke that stops.
wrong.screen: the name strip writes line segment under the stroke, not line, and the tape runs along it and stops at the second dot with a reading. Beside it the ruler draws the same stroke again with an arrowhead at each end, and the tape along that one runs off both edges of the board with its reading blank. Both strokes stay drawn with their names under them, nothing marked.

wrong.why: the drawn part of a line is a definite size on the paper, and a ruler laid against it gives a number as readily as it does for anything else.
wrong.move: measures from one arrowhead to the other and gives that as the length of the line.
wrong.screen: the tape is laid from arrowhead to arrowhead and keeps unrolling past each one, the board sliding to show the line carrying on beyond where it was drawn, while the reading stays blank. The child's number stays in the slot, and the key reading no length is lit on the pad beside it.

phases.screen: two named points on the board with the ruler lying across them and both end caps waiting
phases.soWhat: A line is straight, has an arrowhead at each end and no end points, and has no length that can be measured.
phases.concept: A line goes on for ever both ways

phases.win: the tape stops at the second dot of the segment and reads its length, and on the ray it unrolls off the board
phases.does: runs the tape along each stroke and reads the one length it finds
phases.goal: a line segment has two end points and a length, and a ray has one end point and goes on in one direction
phases.says: Which one can the tape measure? Why does the other one run away?
phases.check: A stroke has a dot at one end and an arrowhead at the other. Name it from the right end. Can a ruler measure it?
phases.feels: a dot says stop and an arrowhead says keep going, and the tape believes them both
phases.hands: Cut one piece of string with a knot at each end, and leave a second piece knotted at one end and still joined to the ball at the other. Ask which one can be laid along a ruler and read. Then draw segment GH and ray MN on the board and let the class say why only one of them has a length.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many dots does the stroke have? Second rung, the phase's: at which end does the tape stop? Third rung: the board is cut to one segment, and one of its dots is swapped for an arrowhead while the tape runs along it. The letter pad and the number pad stay open.

wrong.why: the part of the ray drawn on the paper is short and plainly starts and stops on the page, so it looks as measurable as the segment beside it.
wrong.move: gives ray MN a length, reading the ruler from M to the arrowhead.
wrong.screen: the tape unrolls from the dot at M, passes N and reaches the arrowhead, and keeps on unrolling past it off the board with its reading blank. The segment beside it is measured again and its tape stops at the second dot with a number. The child's length stays in the slot beside the no length key, nothing marked.

wrong.why: a segment can be named from either end, GH or HG, so the order of the letters seems not to matter for a ray either.
wrong.move: names the ray from its arrowhead end, writing ray NM for the ray that starts at M.
wrong.screen: the splitter draws the ray the child's name describes, starting at N and running back through M and on past it in sky blue, a different ray pointing the other way. The drawn ray stays lit starting at M, the two stand side by side with their names under them, and nothing is marked.

phases.screen: two strokes side by side, one capped with a dot at each end and one with a dot and an arrowhead
phases.soWhat: A line segment has two end points and can be measured; a ray has one end point, goes on in one direction and cannot be measured.
phases.concept: A segment has two ends, a ray has one

phases.win: the line lights one way and then the other from the tapped point, and three ray names settle, each starting with its letter
phases.does: taps the middle point, watches the splitter light each way in turn, and names every ray that starts there
phases.goal: a point on a line is the start of two rays, one going each way, each named from that point first
phases.says: Tap the middle point. How many rays start here? Name each one from this point.
phases.check: Mark A, B and C in that order on a line. Name the two rays that start at B.
phases.feels: a point on a line has the line running away from it both ways, and each way is a ray of its own
phases.hands: Stretch a string line across the room and stand a child on it. Ask how many ways they could walk off along the string from where they stand without turning. Two. Tape a card arrow to each end and say that each walk is a ray starting where the child stands. Then mark three points on a drawn line and ask for the rays that start at the middle one.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which point do the rays start at? Second rung, the phase's: which ways can you go along the line from there? Third rung: the board is cut to a line through two points with a third marked between them, and the splitter lights one way before the child names the other. The letter pad stays open.

wrong.why: every ray shown so far was drawn as a separate stroke, so a ray hidden inside a line does not look like a ray at all.
wrong.move: names only ray LP, the one drawn as a stroke of its own, and says there is no second ray to find.
wrong.screen: the splitter lights the line from L one way, out through M to its arrowhead, and holds it lit beside the drawn ray, then lights the other way through K in sky blue. The names ray LM and ray LK write themselves into the strip under the child's one name, which stays where it was written, and nothing is marked.

wrong.why: a line is named by two of its points in either order, and a ray along the line looks as though it should be named the same way.
wrong.move: names the two rays along the line with the starting point last, writing ray KL and ray ML.
wrong.screen: the splitter draws the rays the child's names describe, one starting at K and one starting at M, each in sky blue and each running on through L. The two rays that start at L are lit beside them in deep blue, all four names stand in the strip, and nothing is marked.

phases.screen: a line through three named points, with a fourth point off the line joined to the middle one as a ray
phases.soWhat: A point on a line is the start of two rays, one going each way, and each is named from that point first.
phases.concept: Two rays start at every point on a line

writeup.delight: The fourth phase, the moment the middle point is tapped. The line lights from that point one way, out through the next letter to the arrowhead at the edge, and holds; then it lights the other way in sky blue and holds too, so the one line is seen as two rays pointing apart from one dot. Their names write themselves into the strip, each beginning with the tapped letter, beside the name of the ray that was drawn all along. The tap can be made on any point of the line as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the board is empty, the point stamp stands at its left with the letter tray open under it, and the magnifier rests at the foot of the tool column. On the second two named points stand on the board with the ruler lying across them and both end sockets of the stroke open and empty. On the third two strokes lie one above the other, one capped with a dot at each end and one with a dot and an arrowhead, with the tape coiled at the left hand end of each. On the fourth a line runs across the board through three named points, a fourth point off the line is joined to the middle one as a ray, and the ray splitter waits beside the middle point. The running count at the top left holds what has been named or capped against what this phase lays out, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the point stamp, or an empty socket, or the coiled tape, or the middle point, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks what the end of a stroke says. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any number of points and strokes with any caps, and the tape, the magnifier and the ray splitter open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on points having no size, lines drawn three ways with an arrowhead at each end, telling a segment from a ray, and naming the rays that start at a point on a line.
voiceLines: An empty board, a point stamp and a ruler. What does the end of a stroke tell you?
Put a point down and give it a name. Look closer. Does it get any bigger?
Draw it straight through both points. Now run the tape along it. Where does it stop?
Which one can the tape measure? Why does the other one run away?
Tap the middle point. How many rays start here? Name each one from this point.
A new board. Look at both ends before you name anything.
Free play. Any points, any strokes, any caps, with the tape and the ray splitter open.
Run the tape along it again, and read what each end says.
Every point named, every end capped, and both rays found where only one was drawn.

observations.why: The dot only shows where the point is, and a place has no length and no breadth to grow.
observations.soWhat: A point has no size. A bigger dot is a bigger mark of ink, not a bigger point.
observations.observe: The paper spread apart under the magnifier and the dot stayed one small mark.

observations.why: An arrowhead says the stroke carries on, and something that carries on for ever has no end for the tape to stop at.
observations.soWhat: A line has no end points and no length that can be measured.
observations.observe: The tape ran off both edges of the board along the line and never gave a reading.

observations.why: The segment stopped at both its dots, and the ray stops only at its one end point.
observations.soWhat: A segment can be measured. A ray starts at an end point, goes on in one direction and cannot be measured.
observations.observe: Swapping one dot for an arrowhead took the reading off the tape.

observations.why: A point on a line has the line running away from it both ways, and each way is a ray that starts at that point.
observations.soWhat: A point on a line is the start of two rays, one each way, and each is named from that point first.
observations.observe: The splitter lit two rays from a point where only one ray had been drawn.

phases.screen: an empty drawing board with the point stamp, the letter tray and the magnifier waiting
phases.win: the paper spreads apart under the magnifier while the dot stays one small mark, and the curve runs through every named point in order
phases.traceback: The glass spreads the paper apart while the place each dot marks stays one small mark.
ladder: What does the dot show?
Count the joins between the dots, not the dots.
Look at the place each dot marks, not the ink.
Does the place grow when the ink does?
Look at the middle of the dot. That is the place it marks.

phases.screen: two named points on the board with the ruler lying across them and both end caps waiting
phases.win: the tape runs off both edges of the board without finding an end, and the line is named by its two points
phases.traceback: The tape runs from arrowhead to arrowhead, off both edges of the board, with its reading blank.
ladder: What sits at each end of the stroke now?
Every line takes an arrowhead at both of its ends.
Look at where U and V sit on the board.
Follow the tape past the arrowhead. Does it ever stop?
Only a dot stops the tape. Look at both ends again.

phases.screen: two strokes side by side, one capped with a dot at each end and one with a dot and an arrowhead
phases.win: the tape stops at the second dot of the segment and reads its length, and on the ray it unrolls off the board
phases.traceback: The tape stops at the second dot with a reading, and runs off the board at the arrowhead.
ladder: How many dots does each stroke have?
What does the end you just capped say now?
Look for the end that would stop the tape.
At which end does the tape stop?
A dot says stop. An arrowhead says keep going.

phases.screen: a line through three named points, with a fourth point off the line joined to the middle one as a ray
phases.win: the line lights one way and then the other from the tapped point, and three ray names settle, each starting with its letter
phases.traceback: The splitter lights the line one way and then the other, and every ray name writes itself from that point.
ladder: Which point do the rays start at?
Stand on C and walk each way along the line.
One ray is drawn already. The line itself holds more.
Which ways can you go along the line from there?
Name each ray from the point it starts at.

onWrong.marks: Nothing is marked, nothing resets, no colour means good or bad. The child's answer stays; the pad re-opens after the traceback.
tracebacks: Phase 1: The glass spreads the paper apart while the place each dot marks stays one small mark.
Phase 2: The tape runs from arrowhead to arrowhead, off both edges of the board, with its reading blank.
Phase 3: The tape stops at the second dot with a reading, and runs off the board at the arrowhead.
Phase 4: The splitter lights the line one way and then the other, and every ray name writes itself from that point.

voice.opening: An empty board, a point stamp and a ruler. What does the end of a stroke tell you?
voice.onMiss: the item's own miss line, then the phase's two ladder rungs
voice.onFinish: Every point named, every end capped, and both rays found where only one was drawn.
voice.rules: Spoken on opening, as each phase begins, on each question, on a miss and on the summary page. Every line is printed in the bubble, numbers as words, by the device's own voice (Indian English first). Muting keeps the child's place; unmuting speaks on from the word it reached. If the browser refuses speech until a tap, the first line waits behind a Tap to start cover.

guide.playsOn: none: an Udgam tool opens straight on its phase; the phase's teach lines are spoken first, and a demo phase waits for the child's own act.

palette.rule: A content colour fills countable things only and chrome never borrows one; coloured numerals and words take a deeper ink of their colour (4.5:1).

toolQuestions.source: props.questions ?? props.additionalProps?.questions is read; the authored rows below keep their stage (fitHost returns null).

items.planQuestion: A dot is drawn on a card and named R. Seen through a magnifying glass, the dot looks bigger. Has point R grown?

question.en: Drag the glass over point R. The dot looks bigger under it. What has really grown?

items.planAnswer: No. Point R has no size at all; the dot only shows where it is

items.planQuestion: Five dots are drawn in a row. Name them with capital letters, then join them in order with a curved line. How many curved pieces join one dot to the next?

question.en: Tap each dot to name it and join it to the one before. How many curved pieces do you draw?

items.planAnswer: Four. With the dots named A, B, C, D and E, the pieces go from A to B, B to C, C to D and D to E

items.planQuestion: One point is drawn as a tiny dot and another as a big dot. Which point is bigger?

question.en: One dot is tiny and one is fat. Pass the glass over each. Which point is bigger?

items.planAnswer: Neither. A point has no size, so both dots only mark a place

items.planQuestion: Points C and D are marked on a board. A straight stroke passes through both and has an arrowhead at each end. What is it, and how long is it?

question.en: Give this stroke through C and D an arrowhead at each end. Now how long is it?

items.planAnswer: It is line CD, and it has no length that can be measured, because it goes on for ever both ways

items.planQuestion: Draw four horizontal lines, two vertical lines and two slanting lines. How many arrowheads do you draw altogether?

question.en: Here are lines across, upright and slanting. Tap each one to arrow both its ends. How many arrowheads in all?

items.planAnswer: Sixteen, because each of the eight lines has an arrowhead at both ends

items.planQuestion: Line UV is drawn standing straight up the page. Is it horizontal, vertical or slanting, and what is its length?

question.en: Turn the ruler until it lies through U and V, then let go to draw. Which way does line UV run?

items.planAnswer: It is vertical, and it has no length that can be given, because a line goes on for ever both ways

items.planQuestion: Segment GH has a dot at G and a dot at H. Ray MN has a dot at M and an arrowhead beyond N. Which of them can be measured with a ruler?

question.en: Stroke GH has a dot at each end. Stroke MN has a dot at M and an arrowhead past N. Which one can the tape measure?

items.planAnswer: Segment GH, because it has two end points. Ray MN starts at M and goes on for ever beyond N

items.planQuestion: A stroke has a dot at one end and an arrowhead at the other. Is it a line, a line segment or a ray?

question.en: This stroke has a dot at W. Cap the open end with an arrowhead. What is it then?

items.planAnswer: A ray, because it has one end point and goes on in one direction

items.planQuestion: Segment JK is six centimetres long. The dot at K is swapped for an arrowhead. Can it still be measured?

question.en: Segment JK is six centimetres long. Swap the dot at K for an arrowhead. How long is it now?

items.planAnswer: No. It is now ray JK, which starts at J and goes on for ever beyond K

items.planQuestion: Points E, F and G lie in that order on a line with an arrowhead at each end. Name the two rays that start at F along the line.

question.en: Points E, F and G lie on this line. Tap F, then tap the point each ray runs through.

items.planAnswer: Ray FE and ray FG, one going each way from F

items.planQuestion: Points A, B, C and D lie in that order on a line. Name the two rays that start at C along the line.

question.en: A, B, C and D lie on this line in order. Find the two rays that start at C.

items.planAnswer: Ray CB, which carries on through A, and ray CD, going the other way

items.planQuestion: A line passes through K, L and M in that order. A ray starts at L and passes through P, which is not on the line. Name three rays that start at L.

question.en: A line runs through K, L and M. A ray from L passes through P. Find three rays that start at L.

items.planAnswer: Ray LP, which is drawn, and ray LK and ray LM along the line, one going each way

scoring.wrong: costs nothing, never marked, counted only for first try accuracy
scoring.stars: one for finishing, two at sixty per cent right first time, three at ninety; hidden with the first-try line by showScore false
scoring.phaseMount: a mount scores every phase it plays, from its phase to the last (+5 a question; phases of 3, 3, 3, 3 questions)
scoring.finishCard: stars and the Right first time line under the phase rows on the summary page

hostContract.phase: absent (not a finite number): the whole lesson, phases one to 4 in a row, the summary page at the end, finished once. Present: rounded and clamped to one to 4; the tool starts at that phase and, as the NCERT tools do, walks on by itself after each phase's last question (its closing line, then 1.4 s), in user and AI mode alike, through phase 4 to the summary page; finished once, from the summary page.
hostContract.navigableDots: true (or no phase): user mode, the phase dots are controls; otherwise AI mode, the dots show progress and the agent drives window.toolApi.

onProgress.done: questions right so far in this phase

hostContract.emits: every event is dispatched on window and, when framed, posted to window.parent as { type: 'event', name, detail }

phases.concept: A line goes on for ever both ways
A segment has two ends, a ray has one
Two rays start at every point on a line

getState: toolId, mediaId, mode, mountPhase, phase, phases, conceptId, objectiveIds, step, steps, item, items, stage (teach, demo, ask, win, idle, summary, free), question, questionText, choices, typed, keypadOpen, tries, answered, firstTry, score, maxScore, answerShown (only after the answer), complete, questionCount, muted, speaking, voice, mascot, summaryRow, played, points, strokes, caps, tapeReading, s

terminalEvent.name: finished
terminalEvent.fires: once per mount, from the summary page after the last phase, 5 s after the page opens (its lines may still be going on); one-shot guarded and re-armed by restart or Play again; never sent at the end of an earlier phase (the tool walks on), and never if Free play or Play again is tapped first

sounds: Web Audio, no files: correct, wrong (soft), win, and a tick when a piece snaps

voiceLines.en: An empty board, a point stamp and a ruler. What does the end of a stroke tell you?
Put a point down and give it a name. Look closer. Does it get any bigger?
Draw it straight through both points. Now run the tape along it. Where does it stop?
Which one can the tape measure? Why does the other one run away?
Tap the middle point. How many rays start here? Name each one from this point.
A new board. Look at both ends before you name anything.
Free play. Any points, any strokes, any caps, with the tape and the ray splitter open.
Run the tape along it again, and read what each end says.
Every point named, every end capped, and both rays found where only one was drawn.
